transcript:
This message comes from the UPS Store.
Open this holiday to help with all your small business needs.
Find a store near you at the upsstore.com.
Most locations are independently owned.
Products, services, pricing, and hours of operation may vary.
See Center for details.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Lyndi Kenyon.
President Trump says he's open to working with Democrats
after major Republican losses in the midterm elections.
But NPR's Franco Ordonez reports his decision
to replace White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles
with hardliner Stephen Miller may suggest otherwise.
Stephen Miller is one of the most uncompromising
political ideologues pressing for Trump's agenda.
He is the architect of some of Trump's
most controversial policies, including border policies
and the mass deportation raids that led to
a significant level of political backlash.
Miller is also very loyal, which is something
Trump prizes and means a lot to him,
especially when he's under pressure like he is right now.
Ordonez says even some Republicans have spoken out
against Miller's appointment, questioning whether
he's learned any lessons from the midterms.
The elections ousted Republicans from the majority
in both the House and the Senate.
Negotiators from the U.S., Russia and Ukraine
will meet in Abu Dhabi tomorrow for a new round of peace talks.
Despite objections from the Kremlin,
France says European officials will also attend.
Willem Marx has the story.
- France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Baro said Sunday
his country will certainly be at the talks
alongside other European representatives.
Last week, a Kremlin spokesperson said Europe
could not take part because the three-way format
had already been agreed to.
Concerns about the end goal for negotiations mediated
by the U.S. have grown since President Trump
suggested a coming deal could include, quote,
"more than Ukraine," perhaps involving parts of Europe, too.
In a CNN interview, Ukraine's President Volodymy Zelensky
warned that approach could be, quote, "dangerous."
This will be the fourth round of Trump-brokered talks
and the first since February.
Russia's sending a more senior delegation,
but the two sides remain far apart
on territorial control and security guarantees.
For NPR News, I'm Willem Marx.
- More people these days are turning
to artificial intelligence to discuss deeply personal
concerns ranging from their health to their finances
to their relationships.
But as NPR's Windsor Johnston reports,
those conversations with chatbots
might not be as private as you might think.
- AI companies could potentially read what you type
depending on the service and its settings.
Laurie Craner, a privacy researcher
at Carnegie Mellon University, says,
"Be careful what you disclose."
- If there are things you don't want, say,
your employer to find out about or your friends or family,
you want to be very careful unless you're really sure
that that agent is going to keep it confidential.
- Law enforcement may also obtain chat records,
which could become evidence in a criminal case.
And paying for a subscription
doesn't guarantee confidentiality.
Craner recommends checking privacy controls,
turning off saved memories, and reviewing chat history.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News.
- You're listening to NPR.
A new analysis from a European research group
says China's planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions
sharply declined in the third quarter.
This marks China's biggest drop in emissions
since the start of the COVID pandemic.
NPR's Julia Simon reports.
- What's driving the drop in China's emissions?
One reason?
China is using a lot less oil for transportation.
The country's electrical vehicle fleet continues to grow,
with 67% of passenger car sales now electric.
The country is also growing its renewable energy sector,
namely solar, wind, and batteries.
Goal use is falling in many regions,
and emissions are falling in cement and steel industries.
The United Nations climate talks begin on Monday in Turkey.
China will be at the talks
and is expected to focus on promoting trade
of its solar panels, batteries, and EVs.
The U.S. will not be attending the climate talks.
Julia Simon, NPR News.
- Google, Meta, and TikTok have filed separate lawsuits
seeking to block a California law
designed to protect children from the risks of social media.
The social media companies argue
the law violates their First Amendment rights.
The law is scheduled to go into effect on January 1st.
It prohibits tech companies from offering addictive feeds,
endless scrolling, and auto-played videos to children
under the age of 16.
Governor Gavin Newsom signed the bill into law in September,
and the state's attorney general
vows to vigorously defend it.
I'm Lynda Kenyon, NPR News, in Washington.
- [Announcer] NPR's vital journalism and get NPR+
at plus.npr.org.
That's plus.npr.org.

topics.text: President Trump names hardliner Stephen Miller to replace White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles
US, Russia, and Ukraine negotiators to meet in Abu Dhabi for new peace talks; France says Europe will attend
AI chatbot conversations may not be private, as companies can read chats and law enforcement may obtain them
China's greenhouse gas emissions drop sharply in third quarter, driven by less oil use and growing EV adoption
Google, Meta, and TikTok sue to block California law restricting addictive social media features for children under 16
